title: Food and hosting
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Bringen Sie mir bitte + den/die/das + N

rules.text: Ordering is L1's own vocabulary in a new seat: L1-M3's möchte, M3's accusative article, and M1's dative recipient — Bringen Sie mir bitte die Rechnung. Ich will exists and is blunter than English "I want" quite is, so möchte is what this course writes.

A GERMAN REFUSAL IS TAKEN AT FACE VALUE, and this is the opposite of the Indian, Russian and Italian hosting the other courses in this collection describe. An offer is made once or twice; insisting past a Nein, danke is the impolite move rather than the hospitable one. So the refusal needs no elaborate softening — Nein danke, ich bin satt is complete and warm enough.

Zusammen oder getrennt? is asked at every German table: together or separately. A learner who has never heard the question will not understand the answer they are expected to give, and there is no equivalent moment in a British or American restaurant.

das Essen lands on L1-M3's essen row and cannot do otherwise — the index folds case away, so the noun and the verb are one key. Its note is true of "to eat" and "the meal" alike, and this module writes no new row for it. Write the capital anyway: the index cannot see it, and the reader can.

noch is the offer word — Möchten Sie noch Kaffee? — and it is chosen deliberately so that mehr stays free for M9's comparative. That is the same protection en-es gives más by offering otro and en-fr gives plus by offering encore.

words.note: Speise plus Karte — a food card. Feminine, because Karte is, and the last part always decides.

sentences.trap: einen is the masculine ACCUSATIVE, and it is the only cell of ein that is visibly different. Kaffee is masculine, so the order shows the case — a feminine or neuter thing would hide it.

words.note: It takes two objects like geben: the person in the dative, the thing in the accusative. Regular in the present, though its past is not.
Feminine — every German noun in -ung is. It is also an invoice or a calculation, from rechnen, to reckon.

sentences.trap: The imperative and the ordinary sentence use the same words in a different order. Sie bringen mir is a statement; Bringen Sie mir is a request, and only the position of the verb says which.

words.note: SINGULAR in German — das Gemüse — where English is plural, so its verb is ist. The Ge- prefix makes a collective out of a thing, as Gebäck does with baking.
Masculine. It covers the dish and the leaf alike, so ein Salat can be either.
Masculine, and singular like Gemüse. The ei is the sound of English "eye", so it is not said like the English word.

sentences.trap: Gemüse takes ist and not sind. Translating the English plural gets the verb wrong as well as the noun, and the Ge- prefix is the signal that it is a collective.

sentences.trap: noch is M2's "still" in its other seat: at a table it is the OFFER word, and nothing follows it. noch Kaffee is an unspecified amount, exactly as English's "more coffee" is, and adding einen would make it one more cup specifically.

words.note: Masculine, so einen in the accusative. Its plural is also Teller — the -er ending does not change.
Neuter — das Glas — and its plural umlauts and adds -er. ein Glas Wasser is a glass of water, with no word between the nouns.

sentences.trap: Two objects again, and the dative comes first. mir before einen Teller, exactly as M3's dem Mann came before das Buch — the frame has not changed, only the words in it.
